# The Edwardsville Amazon Warehouse Collapse: A Comprehensive Analysis of the December 10, 2021 Disaster
## 1\. Introduction
On the evening of December 10, 2021, a catastrophic structural failure occurred at the Amazon delivery station identified as DLI4 in Edwardsville, Illinois. The facility, a pivotal node in the e-commerce giant's "last mile" logistics network, was struck by an EF-3 tornado during a historic severe weather outbreak that swept across the central United States. The event resulted in the deaths of six workers, injuries to several others, and the near-total destruction of the facility's southern wing .

The collapse of DLI4 stands as a watershed moment in the intersection of industrial warehousing, labor rights, and climate adaptation. It exposed critical vulnerabilities in "tilt-up" concrete construction methods when subjected to extreme wind loads and highlighted the precarious nature of the gig economy workforce during environmental crises. The tragedy catalyzed a multi-year reevaluation of safety standards, leading to federal investigations by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), complex civil litigation involving questions of premise liability and employment status, and significant legislative reforms such as the Illinois Warehouse Safety Standards Task Force recommendations and the federal Warehouse Worker Protection Act of 2025 .

Writing from the perspective of December 18, 2025, this report provides an exhaustive encyclopedic record of the disaster. It synthesizes forensic engineering data, meteorological timelines, legal testimonies, and the evolving regulatory landscape to offer a definitive account of how a modern logistics facility became the site of one of the deadliest industrial accidents in recent Illinois history.

## 2\. Meteorological Genesis: The Quad-State Tornado Outbreak
To understand the structural failure of the Amazon facility, one must first examine the atmospheric violence that precipitated it. The storm that struck Edwardsville was not an isolated anomaly but part of the "Quad-State Tornado Outbreak," a prolific severe weather event that occurred on December 10-11, 2021\.

### 2.1 Atmospheric Dynamics and Forecasting
December tornadoes are historically rare in the Midwest due to the typical lack of warm, unstable air required for supercell formation. However, on December 10, 2021, a potent trough of low pressure moved from the Rockies into the central Plains, drawing an unseasonably warm and humid air mass northward from the Gulf of Mexico. This created a volatile atmospheric environment characterized by high convective potential energy and strong wind shear—the necessary ingredients for rotating updrafts .

The National Weather Service (NWS) in St. Louis had identified the potential for severe weather well in advance. Forecast models up to three days prior indicated a significant risk, and the office was fully staffed on the evening of the event in anticipation of a major outbreak. The Storm Prediction Center had issued a "Moderate Risk" for the region, a high-level alert that warned of the potential for long-track, intense tornadoes .

### 2.2 The Edwardsville Supercell
As evening fell, discrete supercells initiated across Missouri and Illinois. The specific cell that impacted Edwardsville formed ahead of the main squall line. At approximately 8:27 PM CST, this supercell produced a tornado that touched down near the intersection of Interstate 270 and Illinois Route 255, just southwest of the Amazon facility .

The tornado was rated as an EF-3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale. Post-storm surveys estimated its peak wind speeds at 150 miles per hour . The path of the tornado tracked directly across the Gateway Commerce Center, a sprawling industrial park that housed the Amazon DLI4 station. The width and intensity of the vortex meant that the facility was subjected to wind loads far exceeding the standard design thresholds for commercial structures in that region, though the specifics of the building's failure would later raise questions about construction quality versus wind velocity .

## 3\. The Facility: DLI4 Architectural and Operational Profile
The structure at the center of the tragedy was a modern logistics facility, purpose-built to serve the accelerating demands of e-commerce delivery. Understanding its design is crucial to analyzing the collapse.

### 3.1 Structural Design: Tilt-Up Concrete Construction
The DLI4 facility, located at 3077 Gateway Commerce Center Drive South, was a "delivery station" spanning approximately 1.1 million square feet . It was constructed using "tilt-up" concrete technology, a method ubiquitous in the warehousing industry due to its cost-effectiveness and speed of construction.

In tilt-up construction, large concrete wall panels are cast horizontally on the building's floor slab. Once cured, these panels—often weighing tens of tons and standing 40 feet tall—are tilted vertically by cranes and set into place . They are temporarily braced until the roof structure (the diaphragm) is installed, which ties the walls together and provides lateral stability.

The "Big Box" Vulnerability: 
While code-compliant, tilt-up structures rely heavily on the integrity of the roof-to-wall connections. If the roof is compromised—either by uplift from tornadic winds or by collapse—the heavy concrete walls lose their lateral support and can fall outward or, more deadly, inward. At DLI4, the tornado's winds caused a failure of the roof diaphragm, leading the 40-foot walls on both the east and west sides of the southern wing to collapse inward onto the operations floor .

### 3.2 Operational Role: The Last Mile
DLI4 was not a "fulfillment center" where goods are stored long-term. It was a delivery station, the final stop in Amazon's logistics chain before packages reach the customer. Packages arrived from fulfillment centers via tractor-trailers, were sorted by warehouse associates, and then loaded into delivery vans driven by Delivery Service Partner (DSP) drivers.

This operational role meant the facility was a hub of high-frequency transit. At 8:30 PM on a Friday in December—the height of the "Peak Season" holiday rush—the facility was bustling with activity. DSP drivers were returning from their routes to drop off undelivered packages and return their vans, while warehouse associates were processing the sorting for the next day's deliveries .

### 3.3 The Shelter Deficit
Crucially, the DLI4 facility, like most warehouses built in the region prior to 2022, did not contain a reinforced storm shelter or a basement. The massive footprint of the building and the high water table in parts of Illinois often deter the construction of below-ground shelters. Instead, the facility's Emergency Action Plan (EAP) designated internal restrooms and break areas as "shelter-in-place" zones. These areas were centrally located but were not hardened against EF-3 tornado impacts. They were essentially drywall enclosures within the larger concrete shell .

## 4\. Chronology of the Disaster
The timeline of December 10, 2021, reveals a sequence of warnings, delays, and rapid decisions that determined who lived and who died.

### 4.1 Pre-Impact: The Warning Phase (8:00 PM \- 8:16 PM)
By 8:00 PM, severe storms had entered the Metro East area. Management at DLI4 began monitoring weather feeds. At this time, Amazon's electronic systems and third-party apps began pushing alerts to DSP drivers still on the road .

* **8:06 PM:** The National Weather Service issued the first Tornado Warning for the polygon including the Edwardsville facility. 
* **8:06 PM \- 8:16 PM:** A series of updated warnings confirmed the rotation was tightening and heading toward the industrial park .

It was during this window that the critical failure in communication infrastructure occurred. According to the OSHA investigation, the site's megaphone—intended to be used by managers to marshal employees over the noise of the conveyor belts—was locked in a cage and inaccessible . This forced managers to rely on shouting and hand signals to initiate the evacuation.

### 4.2 The Shelter-in-Place Order (8:16 PM \- 8:26 PM)
Site leadership directed all personnel to the designated safe zones. Because of the facility's size (roughly the length of several football fields), the distance to a shelter could be significant.

* **The North Safe Zone:** The majority of the workers successfully reached the restroom on the north side of the building. This area, by a stroke of structural luck, would remain largely intact during the storm . 
* **The South Safe Zone:** A smaller group of workers, primarily DSP drivers returning from routes and associates working in the southern sorting lanes, were directed to the restroom on the south side. This group included Austin McEwen, Clayton Cope, and others who would ultimately perish .

The OSHA investigation later revealed that some independent contractors were unsure of where the shelter was located, having never participated in a drill at that specific site .

### 4.3 Impact and Collapse (8:27 PM)
At 8:27 PM, the tornado struck. The southern portion of the building took a direct hit. The wind uplift forces tore the roof off the southern wing. Without the roof diaphragm to hold them, the 40-foot tall, 11-inch thick concrete walls buckled and fell inward.

The collapse was immediate and violent. The south restroom, where seven individuals had taken shelter, was crushed under the falling concrete panels. The north restroom, located just outside the path of the worst structural failure, survived, though its occupants were trapped by debris and terrified by the sound of the building disintegrating around them .

## 5\. Casualties: Profiles of the Fallen
The human cost of the collapse was devastating. Six individuals lost their lives, each representing a different facet of the logistics workforce. Their deaths became the focal point for the subsequent legal and legislative battles.

### 5.1 The Victims
1\. Austin J. McEwen (26) 
An independent contractor and driver for a DSP. McEwen was a resident of Edwardsville and was known for his love of sports and music. He was sheltering in the restroom when the walls fell. His death became the subject of the first major wrongful death lawsuit, with his family's attorneys arguing he was "ordered" to stay at the facility rather than evacuate . 
2\. Clayton Lynn Cope (29) 
A maintenance worker from Alton, Illinois. Cope was a Navy veteran. Reports from survivors and family indicated that Cope spent his final moments trying to warn other workers of the approaching storm, delaying his own shelter to ensure others were moving. He was found near the shelter area . 
3\. Deandre S. Morrow (28) 
A driver from St. Louis, Missouri. Morrow was scheduled to have the day off but had picked up an extra shift to earn money for the holidays. He was returning his van when the warnings sounded. His presence at the facility was a direct result of the high-demand "Peak Season" economics . 
4\. Etheria S. Hebb (34) 
A resident of St. Louis, Hebb was a single mother who had recently started working at the facility. She was known for her dedication to her family. Her death left behind a young son, amplifying the tragedy for the community . 
5\. Larry E. Virden (46) 
A father from Collinsville, Illinois. Virden was a driver who had been with his DSP for several months. Just minutes before the tornado struck, he reportedly texted his family that Amazon would not let him leave until the storm passed—a communication that would later be scrutinized in the media, though Amazon maintained that staying put was the safer option during a tornado warning . 
6\. Kevin D. Dickey (62) 
The oldest victim, Dickey was a resident of Carlyle, Illinois. He was a dispatcher and driver who was well-respected by the younger workforce for his mentorship and steady demeanor .

### 5.2 The Injured
In addition to the six fatalities, four other workers were injured, one critically. One survivor was airlifted to a regional trauma center with severe crush injuries . The psychological trauma for the survivors, who spent hours trapped in the rubble in the dark, smelling leaking natural gas, was profound and lasting.

## 6\. The OSHA Investigation: Findings and the "Hazard Alert Letter"
In the immediate aftermath, the U.S. Department of Labor's Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) launched a comprehensive investigation into the collapse. The probe, conducted by the Fairview Heights Area Office, examined whether Amazon and the DSPs had violated federal safety standards .

### 6.1 The Outcome: No Citations
On April 26, 2022, OSHA announced the conclusion of its investigation. To the shock of many labor advocates and victims' families, the agency issued **no citations** and imposed **no monetary penalties** against Amazon or the DSPs.

The agency determined that Amazon's conduct met the *minimum* federal safety guidelines required at the time. Because there was no specific federal standard mandating storm shelters in warehouses or requiring buildings to withstand EF-3 tornadoes, OSHA could not cite Amazon for a violation of a specific rule. The "General Duty Clause"—which requires employers to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards—was deemed insufficient to support a citation in the context of an extreme "Act of God" weather event .

### 6.2 The Hazard Alert Letter (HAL)
While no citations were issued, OSHA utilized a "Hazard Alert Letter" (HAL) to document serious concerns regarding the facility's emergency preparedness. The HAL identified three critical risk factors that, while not illegal under current standards, contributed to the confusion and risk during the event:

1. **Inaccessible Audio Warning Equipment:** The megaphone specified in the Emergency Action Plan (EAP) to alert employees was locked in a cage. Managers could not access it, forcing them to rely on unamplified voice commands in a loud industrial environment. This likely delayed the evacuation of some personnel . 
2. **Lack of Site-Specific Drills:** The investigation revealed that many workers, particularly the transient DSP drivers, did not recall ever participating in severe weather drills at the DLI4 location. They did not know where the "safe zones" were. The EAP was found to be a generic corporate template rather than a plan customized for the specific hazards and layout of Edwardsville . 
3. **Ambiguous Shelter Identification:** The designated shelter areas were not clearly identified with signage that was visible to all workers, specifically those on the transient delivery side of operations .

The HAL effectively put Amazon on notice: while they were not fined for the 2021 collapse, failure to address these specific issues in the future could lead to "willful" violations in subsequent inspections .

## 7\. Forensic Engineering and Structural Analysis
Parallel to the OSHA investigation, attorneys for the victims' families commissioned private forensic engineering studies to determine why the building failed so catastrophically. These reports formed the backbone of the civil litigation.

### 7.1 The "Pinned Column" Hypothesis
A report released by attorneys for the McEwen family, produced by a structural engineer who examined the site immediately after the collapse, alleged serious defects in the construction of the support columns. The engineer noted that a "considerable number" of the columns appeared to have been lifted cleanly out of the floor slab .

The report claimed that the columns lacked proper vertical anchoring. Instead of being bolted or welded to the foundation to resist uplift forces, the report alleged they were merely "pegged" in place or secured with a "bead of caulk." In high-wind events, uplift forces (suction created by the wind passing over the roof) can pull the roof structure upwards. If the columns are not anchored to the ground, they can be lifted along with the roof, or if the roof detaches, the columns lose stability and tip over.

### 7.2 Code Compliance vs. Survivability
Defense experts for Amazon and the construction firms (Contegra and TriStar) argued that the building was constructed in full compliance with the International Building Code (IBC) applicable at the time (2018 edition). They maintained that the code did not require resistance to EF-3 tornado wind speeds (150 mph) for standard commercial structures. The design wind speed for the region was significantly lower, intended to withstand severe thunderstorms but not direct tornado strikes.

This clash highlighted a systemic issue in industrial building codes: the disparity between "life safety" (preventing collapse in standard events) and "asset protection" or "disaster resilience" (surviving extreme events). The Edwardsville collapse demonstrated that code-compliant tilt-up structures could suffer "progressive collapse" where the failure of the roof diaphragm leads to the total loss of wall stability .

## 8\. Civil Litigation: The Quest for Accountability
The legal aftermath of the collapse was defined by a series of high-profile wrongful death and personal injury lawsuits filed in the Circuit Court of Madison County, Illinois.

### 8.1 The Lawsuits
* **McEwen v. Amazon et al.:** Filed in January 2022 by Clifford Law Offices, this suit named Amazon, Amazon Logistics, Contegra Construction, and TriStar Properties as defendants. It alleged negligence in failing to evacuate the facility despite 36 hours of warning and premises liability regarding the structural defects . 
* **Consolidated Cases:** Subsequent lawsuits were filed by the families of Deandre Morrow, Clayton Cope, and others, eventually being consolidated for discovery. Prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump joined the legal team for the Morrow family, framing the issue as one of worker exploitation in minority communities .

### 8.2 The "Independent Contractor" Defense
A central legal battleground was Amazon's use of the "independent contractor" shield. Amazon argued that drivers like McEwen and Morrow were employees of the DSPs (e.g., "Xseed Delivery" or "Boxify Logistics"), not Amazon, and thus Amazon could not be sued for employer negligence under workers' compensation exclusivity rules.

However, plaintiffs argued that Amazon exercised "retained control" over the drivers—dictating their routes, monitoring their speed via apps, setting their schedules, and enforcing safety rules. This, they argued, made Amazon a *de facto* employer or at least a joint employer liable for their safety decisions, particularly the decision to keep drivers on the road as the storm approached .

### 8.3 Settlements (2024-2025)
By late 2024 and throughout 2025, the litigation moved toward resolution.

* **McEwen Settlement:** Public records and legal reporting indicated that the McEwen family reached settlements with the defendants. One specific disbursement approved by a judge in 2024 involved a $250,000 partial settlement from the construction/developer entities, though the total global settlement amount with Amazon was likely much higher and kept confidential under non-disclosure agreements . 
* **Global Resolution:** By December 2025, most of the wrongful death claims had been settled, allowing families to receive compensation without the uncertainty of a jury trial. The settlements effectively closed the civil chapter of the tragedy without a court ruling that would definitively set a precedent on the DSP liability issue .

## 9\. Legislative Reforms: The Illinois Task Force and the WWPA
While the courts handled financial restitution, the political system addressed the regulatory gaps exposed by the disaster.

### 9.1 The Illinois Warehouse Safety Standards Task Force
In response to the tragedy, the Illinois General Assembly passed the Warehouse Safety Standards Task Force Act (Public Act 102-1115). The Task Force, championed by Representatives Katie Stuart (D-Edwardsville) and Jay Hoffman, spent two years studying the issue.

The Final Report (2025): 
Released in early 2025, the Task Force's final report made sweeping recommendations that have since begun to reshape the state's building codes:

1. **Mandatory Tornado Shelters:** The report recommended that Illinois amend its adoption of the International Building Code to *require* tornado-resilient shelters (compliant with ICC 500 standards) in all new warehouse facilities exceeding a certain square footage or occupancy. This was a direct rebuke of the "restroom shelter" strategy used at DLI4.4 
2. **Structural Integrity:** It called for tighter inspections of tilt-up panel connections and roof diaphragms during construction. 
3. **Communication Protocols:** The report mandated that all warehouses must have a site-specific emergency plan that is shared with local fire and police departments, ensuring first responders know the layout and shelter locations before a disaster strikes .

### 9.2 The Federal Warehouse Worker Protection Act (2025)
At the federal level, the Edwardsville collapse energized the movement for the **Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA)**. Introduced in the 118th Congress and reintroduced in the 119th Congress (2025-2026) as **S. 2613** and **H.R. 4896**, the bill represents the most significant federal attempt to regulate the logistics industry .

**Key Provisions (Status as of Dec 2025):**

* **Quota Transparency:** The bill forces companies to disclose productivity quotas to employees and prohibits quotas that prevent workers from taking bathroom breaks or following safety protocols . 
* **Emergency Pause:** While the bill focuses heavily on ergonomic injuries (the "churn and burn" issue), provisions were added following Edwardsville to protect workers who refuse to work under unsafe environmental conditions, effectively codifying a "right to shelter" without fear of retaliation for "Time Off Task" (TOT) violations . 
* **Enforcement:** The bill empowers OSHA with greater oversight capabilities regarding ergonomic hazards and quota-driven safety violations.

Senator Ed Markey and Representative Donald Norcross, sponsors of the bill, frequently cited the Edwardsville six as martyrs of a system that prioritized delivery speed over human life. As of December 18, 2025, the bill had advanced through committee and was pending floor votes, reflecting a sustained bipartisan interest in curbing the excesses of the warehouse boom .

## 10\. Corporate Policy Evolution: The Phone Ban and Safety Drills
The disaster forced Amazon to alter several internal policies that had long been points of contention with its workforce.

### 10.1 The Mobile Phone Policy
Prior to the tornado, Amazon maintained a strict ban on personal cell phones on the warehouse floor, citing security and productivity. The ban had been relaxed during the COVID-19 pandemic but was scheduled to be reinstated in early 2022\.

Survivors of the Edwardsville collapse recounted how their phones were lifelines—allowing them to receive weather alerts that the facility's internal system delayed, and to say goodbye to loved ones when they thought they would die. The public outcry over the idea of workers being trapped without communication forced Amazon's hand.

**2025 Status:** Amazon permanently reversed the ban, allowing workers to carry phones. However, in late 2025, the company introduced new "phone registration" policies to track asset security and differentiate between personal and work usage, reigniting privacy concerns among the workforce .

### 10.2 Emergency Preparedness
Following the OSHA HAL, Amazon implemented a standardized "Severe Weather Policy" across its network. This included:

* **Mandatory Drills:** Increased frequency of severe weather drills, with specific requirements to include DSP drivers and temporary staff. 
* **Badge Cards:** Distribution of "safety cards" to all associates and drivers containing maps of the facility's safe zones. 
* **Audible Alerts:** Upgrades to PA systems and the provision of accessible megaphones in all operational areas to prevent the communication blackout seen at DLI4.12

## 11\. Broader Implications and Future Outlook
The Edwardsville collapse was a tragedy of timing, engineering, and economics. It occurred at the precise moment when the "just-in-time" logistics model collided with the new reality of climate instability.

### 11.1 Climate Change and "Tornado Alley"
Meteorologists have noted a shift in "Tornado Alley" from the Great Plains eastward into the Mississippi River Valley and the Southeast. This region—covering Illinois, Kentucky, and Tennessee—is also a primary corridor for logistics hubs due to its proximity to major interstates and population centers. The Edwardsville disaster demonstrated that the logistical infrastructure of the US is increasingly located in the crosshairs of severe weather, necessitating a rethinking of how these "temporary" tilt-up structures are engineered .

### 11.2 The Rise of Labor Organizing
The tragedy became a potent symbol for the burgeoning labor movement within Amazon. The Amazon Labor Union (ALU) and groups like Amazonians United frequently referenced the "Edwardsville Six" in their organizing campaigns. The argument was visceral: a union contract could legally enshrine the right to stop work during a tornado warning, removing the decision from distant algorithms or managers under pressure to meet quotas. While unionization efforts have faced stiff resistance, the memory of Edwardsville remains a rallying cry for worker safety advocacy .

## 12\. Conclusion
The Amazon warehouse collapse of December 10, 2021, was not merely an accident; it was a systemic failure. It revealed the inadequacy of standard building codes for large-occupancy industrial structures, the dangerous ambiguity of the DSP employment model, and the lethal consequences of prioritizing efficiency over resilience.

By December 2025, the site of DLI4 has been cleared and the logistics network has moved on, but the legal and regulatory landscape has been irrevocably altered. The settlements provided some measure of justice to the families of Austin McEwen, Clayton Cope, Deandre Morrow, Etheria Hebb, Larry Virden, and Kevin Dickey. The Illinois Task Force recommendations and the pending federal Warehouse Worker Protection Act represent a belated but necessary attempt to ensure that the "Last Mile" does not become the final mile for the workers who power the American economy.

The legacy of Edwardsville is a new industrial mandate: that the safety of the human beings inside the box must matter more than the speed of the package leaving it.

The north restroom, located just outside the path of the worst structural failure, survived.
The occupants of the north restroom were trapped by debris and terrified by the sound of the building disintegrating around them.
Austin J. McEwen (26) was an independent contractor and driver for a DSP.
Austin J. McEwen was a resident of Edwardsville and was known for his love of sports and music.
Austin J. McEwen was sheltering in the restroom when the walls fell.
Austin J. McEwen's death became the subject of the first major wrongful death lawsuit.
Austin J. McEwen's family's attorneys argued he was "ordered" to stay at the facility rather than evacuate.
Clayton Lynn Cope (29) was a maintenance worker from Alton, Illinois.
Clayton Lynn Cope was a Navy veteran.

Reports from survivors and family indicated that Clayton Lynn Cope spent his final moments trying to warn other workers of the approaching storm, delaying his own shelter to ensure others were moving.
Clayton Lynn Cope was found near the shelter area.
Deandre S. Morrow (28) was a driver from St. Louis, Missouri.
Deandre S. Morrow was scheduled to have the day off but had picked up an extra shift to earn money for the holidays.
Deandre S. Morrow was returning his van when the warnings sounded.
Deandre S. Morrow's presence at the facility was a direct result of the high-demand "Peak Season" economics.
Etheria S. Hebb (34) was a resident of St. Louis.
Etheria S. Hebb was a single mother who had recently started working at the facility.
Etheria S. Hebb was known for her dedication to her family.
Etheria S. Hebb's death left behind a young son, amplifying the tragedy for the community.
Larry E. Virden (46) was a father from Collinsville, Illinois.
Larry E. Virden was a driver who had been with his DSP for several months.
Just minutes before the tornado struck, Larry E. Virden reportedly texted his family that Amazon would not let him leave until the storm passed.
Kevin D. Dickey (62) was the oldest victim of the collapse.
Kevin D. Dickey was a resident of Carlyle, Illinois.
Kevin D. Dickey was a dispatcher and driver who was well-respected by the younger workforce for his mentorship and steady demeanor.
In addition to the six fatalities, four other workers were injured, one critically.
One survivor of the collapse was airlifted to a regional trauma center with severe crush injuries.
On April 26, 2022, OSHA announced the conclusion of its investigation into the DLI4 collapse.
OSHA issued no citations and imposed no monetary penalties against Amazon or the DSPs.
OSHA determined that Amazon's conduct met the minimum federal safety guidelines required at the time.

Because there was no specific federal standard mandating storm shelters in warehouses or requiring buildings to withstand EF-3 tornadoes, OSHA could not cite Amazon for a violation of a specific rule.

The "General Duty Clause," which requires employers to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards, was deemed insufficient to support a citation in the context of an extreme "Act of God" weather event.
While no citations were issued, OSHA utilized a "Hazard Alert Letter" (HAL) to document serious concerns regarding the DLI4 facility's emergency preparedness.
The Hazard Alert Letter (HAL) identified three critical risk factors that contributed to the confusion and risk during the event, though they were not illegal under current standards.
The megaphone specified in the Emergency Action Plan (EAP) to alert employees was locked in a cage and inaccessible.
Managers could not access the megaphone, forcing them to rely on unamplified voice commands in a loud industrial environment.
The inaccessibility of the megaphone likely delayed the evacuation of some personnel.
The OSHA investigation revealed that many workers, particularly the transient DSP drivers, did not recall ever participating in severe weather drills at the DLI4 location.
Many workers at DLI4 did not know where the "safe zones" were.
The Emergency Action Plan (EAP) at DLI4 was found to be a generic corporate template rather than a plan customized for the specific hazards and layout of Edwardsville.
The designated shelter areas at DLI4 were not clearly identified with signage that was visible to all workers, specifically those on the transient delivery side of operations.
The Hazard Alert Letter (HAL) effectively put Amazon on notice that failure to address these specific issues in the future could lead to "willful" violations in subsequent inspections.
A report released by attorneys for the McEwen family alleged serious defects in the construction of the support columns at DLI4.
A structural engineer who examined the DLI4 site immediately after the collapse noted that a "considerable number" of the columns appeared to have been lifted cleanly out of the floor slab.
The Edwardsville collapse demonstrated that code-compliant tilt-up structures could suffer "progressive collapse" where the failure of the roof diaphragm leads to the total loss of wall stability.
The McEwen v. Amazon et al. lawsuit was filed in January 2022 by Clifford Law Offices.
The McEwen v. Amazon et al. suit named Amazon, Amazon Logistics, Contegra Construction, and TriStar Properties as defendants.
The McEwen v. Amazon et al. lawsuit alleged negligence in failing to evacuate the facility despite 36 hours of warning.
The McEwen v. Amazon et al. lawsuit alleged premises liability regarding the structural defects.
Subsequent lawsuits were filed by the families of Deandre Morrow, Clayton Cope, and others, eventually being consolidated for discovery.
Prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump joined the legal team for the Morrow family.
Ben Crump framed the issue as one of worker exploitation in minority communities.
A central legal battleground was Amazon's use of the "independent contractor" shield.
Amazon argued that drivers like McEwen and Morrow were employees of the DSPs, not Amazon.
Amazon argued that it could not be sued for employer negligence under workers' compensation exclusivity rules because drivers were employees of DSPs.
Plaintiffs argued that Amazon exercised "retained control" over the drivers, dictating their routes, monitoring their speed via apps, setting their schedules, and enforcing safety rules.

Plaintiffs argued that Amazon's retained control made it a de facto employer or at least a joint employer liable for drivers' safety decisions, particularly the decision to keep drivers on the road as the storm approached.
Public records and legal reporting indicated that the McEwen family reached settlements with the defendants.
One specific disbursement approved by a judge in 2024 involved a $250,000 partial settlement from the construction/developer entities.
By December 2025, most of the wrongful death claims had been settled.
The settlements allowed families to receive compensation without the uncertainty of a jury trial.
The settlements effectively closed the civil chapter of the tragedy without a court ruling that would definitively set a precedent on the DSP liability issue.
The Illinois Warehouse Safety Standards Task Force Act (Public Act 102-1115) was passed in response to the DLI4 tragedy.

The Task Force's final report, released in early 2025, recommended that Illinois amend its adoption of the International Building Code to require tornado-resilient shelters (compliant with ICC 500 standards) in all new warehouse facilities exceeding a certain square footage or occupancy.
The recommendation for mandatory tornado shelters was a direct rebuke of the "restroom shelter" strategy used at DLI4.
The Task Force's report mandated that all warehouses must have a site-specific emergency plan that is shared with local fire and police departments.
The site-specific emergency plan ensures first responders know the layout and shelter locations before a disaster strikes.
At the federal level, the Edwardsville collapse energized the movement for the Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA).
The Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA) was introduced in the 118th Congress and reintroduced in the 119th Congress (2025-2026) as S. 2613 and H.R. 4896.
The Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA) represents the most significant federal attempt to regulate the logistics industry.
The Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA) forces companies to disclose productivity quotas to employees.
The Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA) prohibits quotas that prevent workers from taking bathroom breaks or following safety protocols.
Provisions were added to the Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA) following Edwardsville to protect workers who refuse to work under unsafe environmental conditions.
The Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA) effectively codifies a "right to shelter" without fear of retaliation for "Time Off Task" (TOT) violations.

Senator Ed Markey and Representative Donald Norcross, sponsors of the Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA), frequently cited the Edwardsville six as martyrs of a system that prioritized delivery speed over human life.
As of December 18, 2025, the Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA) had advanced through committee and was pending floor votes.
The advancement of the WWPA reflects a sustained bipartisan interest in curbing the excesses of the warehouse boom.
Amazon permanently reversed the ban on personal cell phones, allowing workers to carry phones.
In late 2025, Amazon introduced new "phone registration" policies to track asset security and differentiate between personal and work usage, reigniting privacy concerns among the workforce.
Amazon implemented a standardized "Severe Weather Policy" across its network following the OSHA Hazard Alert Letter (HAL).
Amazon's standardized "Severe Weather Policy" included increased frequency of severe weather drills, with specific requirements to include DSP drivers and temporary staff.
Amazon's standardized "Severe Weather Policy" included the distribution of "safety cards" to all associates and drivers containing maps of the facility's safe zones.
Amazon's standardized "Severe Weather Policy" included upgrades to PA systems and the provision of accessible megaphones in all operational areas to prevent the communication blackout seen at DLI4.
Meteorologists have noted a shift in "Tornado Alley" from the Great Plains eastward into the Mississippi River Valley and the Southeast.
The region covering Illinois, Kentucky, and Tennessee is a primary corridor for logistics hubs due to its proximity to major interstates and population centers.
The Edwardsville disaster demonstrated that the logistical infrastructure of the US is increasingly located in the crosshairs of severe weather.
The Edwardsville disaster necessitates a rethinking of how "temporary" tilt-up structures are engineered.
The DLI4 tragedy became a potent symbol for the burgeoning labor movement within Amazon.
The Amazon Labor Union (ALU) and groups like Amazonians United frequently referenced the "Edwardsville Six" in their organizing campaigns.
A union contract could legally enshrine the right to stop work during a tornado warning, removing the decision from distant algorithms or managers under pressure to meet quotas.
While unionization efforts have faced stiff resistance, the memory of Edwardsville remains a rallying cry for worker safety advocacy.
The first Wrongful Death Suit (McEwen) was filed on January 17, 2022.
The McEwen lawsuit initiated the legal battle over negligence and DSP status.
The OSHA Investigation concluded on April 26, 2022.
No citations were issued by OSHA, but a Hazard Alert Letter (HAL) was released.
The Formation of the IL Warehouse Safety Task Force occurred in 2023.
The IL Warehouse Safety Task Force was a legislative response to study building codes.
The Introduction of the Warehouse Worker Protection Act (WWPA) at the Federal level occurred in 2024.
The WWPA was the first major federal bill addressing warehouse quotas and safety.
The IL Task Force Final Report was released in January 2025.
The IL Task Force Final Report recommended mandatory tornado shelters in warehouses.
The Reintroduction of WWPA (S. 2613) occurred in July 2025.
The reintroduction of WWPA (S. 2613) represented a renewed federal push for worker protection.
Global Settlements were reached in late 2025.
The global settlements resolved major civil litigation claims.
Xseed Delivery LLC employed several victims at DLI4.
Xseed Delivery LLC was investigated by OSHA.
Xseed Delivery LLC was a defendant in civil suits.
Boxify Logistics LLC employed drivers at the DLI4 site.
Boxify Logistics LLC was investigated by OSHA.
AB&C D.A.D. Inc. employed drivers at the DLI4 site.
AB&C D.A.D. Inc. was investigated by OSHA.

**Abstract:** At 8:27 p.m. on December 10, 2021, Employees were performing end of shift duties, some returning vehicles after completion of delivery routes and a tornado struck the Amazon DLI4 delivery facility, located in Edwardsville, IL. Severe storms had entered the area at approximately 8:00 pm. Management at the site began notifying contracted delivery company dispatchers to decide if delivery drivers would return to the site or seek shelter at their locations. Electronic warning systems delivered storm and tornado warnings to the site, between the periods of 8:06 pm and 8:16 pm, via a web-based application. After the alerts, the on-site manager and accompanying process assistant began running through the warehouse and shouting in order to get employees to the northern end of the building, where a tornado shelter had been designated. At approximately 8:18 pm, tornado sirens sounded in the Edwardsville, IL area. Approximately 10 people did not take shelter at the northern end of the building, and sought shelter in a restroom at the southern end. At approximately 8:27 pm, a tornado touched down in front of the delivery facility; cut through the building, moving in a west to east direction; and, lifted just after it reached the end of the property line. The tornado lifted the roof of the building, which caused a section of the southwest wall to fall inward, and a section of the southeast wall to fall outward. The section of the collapsed southwest wall fell on the restroom at the southern end, where the employees took shelter, which caused the restroom to be crushed. Of the 10 workers located within the restroom, six were killed due to crushing, and one was critically injured and hospitalized. Three were trapped, but rescued with minor abrasions. All remaining personnel were evacuated from the building, after the site was cleared by emergency responders.

**Keywords:** Blunt force trauma, Building Collapse, Crushed, Weather

4.title: Task Force Recommends Tornado Shelters in Warehouse Following Deadly 2021 Storm
4.description: Six people were killed when an EF3 tornado with 150 mph winds struck an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville on Dec. 10, 2021. The incident raised questions about the safety of warehouses in severe weather, including if warehouses are designed to withstand extreme winds and if warehouse operators are properly prepared for severe weather.

Task Force Recommends Tornado Shelters in Warehouse Following Deadly 2021 Storm
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Ben Szalinski — Capitol News Illinois](https://news.wttw.com/stories-by-author/ben%20szalinski%20%E2%80%94%20capitol%20news%20illinois) | January 3, 2025, 6:21 pm

[](https://news.wttw.com/#facebook)[](https://news.wttw.com/#twitter)[](https://news.wttw.com/#flipboard)[](https://news.wttw.com/#email)

![Image 10: A survey photo shows the damage to an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville following an EF3 tornado on Dec. 10, 2021. (Photo provided by the National Weather Service)](https://news.wttw.com/sites/default/files/styles/full/public/field/image/Edwardsville%20tornado_CREDIT_NationalWeatherService.jpg?itok=Z1-JTUZl)A survey photo shows the damage to an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville following an EF3 tornado on Dec. 10, 2021. (Photo provided by the National Weather Service)

SPRINGFIELD — A task force created in the wake of a deadly Metro East tornado has issued recommendations for better protecting warehouse workers.

Six people were killed when an EF3 tornado with 150 mph winds struck an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville on Dec. 10, 2021. The incident raised questions about the safety of warehouses in severe weather, including if warehouses are designed to withstand extreme winds and if warehouse operators are properly prepared for severe weather.

Illinois lawmakers established the Warehouse Safety Standards Task Force in January 2023 to study warehouse safety in response to the Edwardsville tornado, and it issued its final report last month.

Among its [recommendations](https://labor.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/idol/documents/warehouse-task-force/Warehouse%20Safety%20Task%20Force%20Final%20Report%2012.19.24%20(002).pdf) was that building codes be amended to require tornado shelters in warehouses. The [International Building Code](https://codes.iccsafe.org/content/IBC2024P1) became Illinois’ statewide building code on Jan. 1 after being approved by the legislature in 2023. The task force recommended shelters be added to that code.

The IBC doesn’t have specific requirements for severe weather because threats vary around the world, Tim Schmitz from the International Code Council told the task force. However, communities can adopt their own codes specifically to meet the needs of natural disasters in their area.

Providing the right shelter from tornadoes can save lives, Greg Bryant from the Masonry Structural Coalition told the task force. He pointed to a [2004 F4 tornado in Woodford County](https://www.weather.gov/ilx/13jul04) that destroyed a manufacturing plant, but all 140 people in the building made it out alive after taking refuge in a designated safe area of the building.

The six people killed in Edwardsville were not in a safe area of the warehouse, Edwardsville police said after the tornado.

The 2021 tornado hit around 8:30 p.m. as the facility was bustling ahead of the holidays. According to the [National Weather Service](https://www.weather.gov/lsx/12_10_2021), the tornado touched down near I-270 and Illinois Route 255 southwest of the warehouse and traveled through the south half of the building. The tornado first impacted the west-facing wall, causing it to collapse. That caused other structural failures, including the roof to collapse. The tornado was on the ground for just five minutes, but debris from Amazon was found miles away from the warehouse after the tornado lifted.

An Occupational Safety and Health Administration investigation into Amazon did not find any violations, according to the task force report. OSHA recommended the company review its severe weather procedures, ensure employees are provided training and participate in drills, have site-specific information about severe weather plans, and ensure audible warning devices are accessible. The warehouse was rebuilt and [reopened in September](https://www.stlpr.org/economy-business/2024-09-17/edwardsville-amazon-warehouse-ravaged-by-2021-tornado-that-killed-6-has-reopened) 2024.

The task force also recommended requiring site-specific emergency plans based on OSHA’s guidelines for employers to prepare for tornadoes. The plans would be shared with local first responders and would include floor plans and details about what is stored in the warehouse.

Illinois saw a record of 142 tornadoes in 2024, [according to the National Weather Service](https://x.com/NWSChicago/status/1874119346659934561). The state has [averaged 60 tornadoes](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/ustormaps/2014-2023-stateavgtornadoes.png) each year over the last 10 years. But the number of tornadoes in the state could be increasing as technology to detect them improves, according to [data compiled by The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/12/18/us/tornadoes-2024.html). Most Illinois counties saw an increase in tornadoes in the 20 years from 2002 to 2022compared to the previous 20 years.

Most tornadoes are not as powerful as the Edwardsville tornado, Marc Levitan from the National Windstorm Impact Reduction Project told the task force, but warehouses are more vulnerable because they’re tall and supported by heavy walls that rely on the roof for stability.

Levitan told the task force it is better to design buildings to withstand the more common modest tornadoes, and buildings should be constructed either with a shelter inside or with a more wind resistant exterior structure. The National Weather Service in Chicago [reported](https://x.com/NWSChicago/status/1874119346659934561) all but one of northeast Illinois’ 63 tornadoes in 2024 had winds of 110 mph or less.

First responders also need more assistance responding to tornadoes, retired Edwardsville Fire Chief James Whiteford told the task force.

The task force agreed with his recommendation that the General Assembly provide regular funding to the Mutual Aid Box Alarm System. MABAS is a series of intergovernmental agreements between Illinois fire departments to bring additional or specialized support to major incidents. MABAS calls range from dispatching additional units to a structure fire to long-term disaster response missions, including outside Illinois. The system received a $200,000 grant from the Office of the State Fire Marshall in fiscal year 2024.
